n: King Lamoni has his servants testify about everything they saw at the waters of Sebus.

f.g: Formally report as witnesses.

n: Hearing of Ammon’s faithfulness and power, Lamoni wonders whether Ammon is the “Great Spirit” — come to punish the people for their killings.

f.g: The Lamanites’ traditional name for God.

n: The servants don’t know whether he is the Great Spirit or a man, but they know he can’t be killed and is clearly the king’s friend.
Lamoni concludes Ammon is the Great Spirit, come to save the servants from being killed as their predecessors were.

f.w: of whom our fathers have spoken
f.g: Lamoni has some inherited belief in God, though incomplete.

n: Lamoni’s tradition taught a Great Spirit but also that whatever they did was right. Now he fears he did wrong in executing his servants — his conscience awakens.

f.w: they supposed that whatsoever they did was right

n: He had killed many servants because thieves scattered their flocks.
Mormon explains: scattering flocks at Sebus was a deliberate tactic so thieves could drive strays to their own land.

f.g: Organized theft.

n: Lamoni asks where this powerful man is.

f.g: Lamoni is eager to meet him.

n: He is feeding the king’s horses — preparing the chariots as Lamoni had ordered for a trip to his father’s great feast in the land of Nephi.

f.g: Horses appear in the Book of Mormon; how they relate to known animals of the ancient Americas is debated.

f.w: the father of Lamoni, who was king over all the land

n: Lamoni is even more amazed: no servant had ever been so faithful, remembering every command even after such an event.

f.w: he doth remember all my commandments
f.g: Ammon’s quiet faithfulness impresses Lamoni as much as his power.

n: Lamoni is sure Ammon is the Great Spirit, and wants to see him but is afraid to ask.

f.g: I dare not.

n: When Ammon comes in, he notices the king’s expression has changed and starts to withdraw.

f.w: the countenance of the king was changed
f.g: His face showed alarm or awe.

n: A servant addresses Ammon as “Rabbanah” — “powerful or great king” — and asks him to stay.

f.g: Mormon translates it “powerful or great king”; compare Hebrew rab, “great,” and rabbi.

n: Ammon asks how he can serve. The king is speechless for an hour.

f.g: Mormon notes the Lamanites measured time their own way.

n: Ammon asks again; still no answer.

f.g: Ammon keeps offering service.

n: Filled with the Spirit, Ammon perceives the king’s thoughts and names what is troubling him.

f.w: he perceived the thoughts of the king

n: Ammon insists he is just a man and Lamoni’s servant, ready to do whatever is right.

f.w: I am a man, and am thy servant

n: Amazed that Ammon can read his mind, Lamoni finally asks: are you the Great Spirit who knows all things?
Ammon simply says no — refusing to take honor that belongs to God.
Lamoni asks how he knows his thoughts and by what power he fought the thieves.

f.g: An open invitation to teach.

n: Lamoni promises Ammon anything he wants — even his army’s protection, though he knows Ammon is stronger.
Ammon, wise yet harmless, asks for only one thing: that the king listen to his words.
Lamoni promises to believe everything — Ammon has won him with wise, honest strategy.

f.g: Guile usually means deceit; here it means a clever approach, as Ammon’s request was honest.

n: Ammon begins teaching boldly: do you believe there is a God?

f.w: Believest thou that there is a God
f.g: Ammon starts with the most basic truth.

n: Lamoni doesn’t know the word “God.”

f.w: I do not know what that meaneth
f.g: Ammon must find common ground in Lamoni’s own vocabulary.

n: So Ammon starts from what Lamoni does know: do you believe in a Great Spirit?

f.g: A wise teacher builds on what the learner already understands.

n: Lamoni says yes.

f.g: Common ground established.

n: Ammon connects the two: the Great Spirit is God. Did he create everything in heaven and earth?
Lamoni believes God created the earth but doesn’t understand “heaven.”

f.w: I do not know the heavens
f.g: An honest admission.

n: Ammon explains: heaven is where God and his holy angels dwell.
Lamoni asks whether it is above the earth.

f.g: A simple, sincere question.

n: Yes — and God looks down on all people, knowing every thought, for he created them all.

f.w: he knows all the thoughts and intents of the heart

n: Lamoni believes, and asks whether Ammon is sent from God.
Ammon explains he is a man, created in God’s image like all people, and called by the Spirit to teach truth.

f.w: created after the image of God

n: A portion of God’s Spirit dwells in him, giving knowledge and power according to his faith.
Ammon teaches from the beginning: the Creation, Adam, the Fall, and the scriptures down to Lehi’s departure from Jerusalem.

f.g: Recounted; told in order.

n: He recounts their ancestors’ wilderness journey and hardships to the king and his servants.

f.w: journeyings of their fathers in the wilderness

n: He tells of the rebellions of Laman, Lemuel, and Ishmael’s sons, and explains the records from Lehi to the present — the Lamanites’ own history from the other side.

f.w: the rebellions of Laman and Lemuel

n: Most importantly, he explains the plan of redemption and the coming of Christ.
The king believes all of it.

f.w: the king believed all his words

n: Lamoni cries out to the Lord for mercy on himself and his people, as God had shown mercy to the Nephites.
Then he falls to the ground as though dead — overcome by the Spirit.
His servants carry him to his wife. For two days and nights he lies as if dead while his family mourns.

f.g: Compare Alma the Younger’s similar experience.
